appraisal_events.evidence: comment peux-tu dire que tu n'as pas eu de plaisir, ta grand'mère nous a raconté que tu ne perdais pas un mot de ce que la Berma disait... / Si elle est très bien, qu'est-ce qu'il te faut de plus ?
appraisal_events.explanation: The father, worried about the awkward impression the narrator's admission of disappointment made on Norpois, publicly defends the boy's genuine rapt attention during the play, but does so with visible impatience, also minimizing the narrator's expressed reservations.

appraisal_events.evidence: dit Norpois en se tournant avec application vers ma mère pour ne pas la laisser en dehors de la conversation et afin de remplir consciencieusement son devoir de politesse envers une maîtresse de maison
appraisal_events.explanation: Norpois deliberately turns to include the mother in the conversation, treating her with formal courtesy as the hostess, positioning her within the valued social exchange rather than as a silent bystander.

status_effects.explanation: The father's defense, citing the grandmother's account of his rapt attention, works to reinstate the narrator as a genuine appreciator of la Berma before Norpois, softening the risk of embarrassment from his earlier admission, though the effect is tempered by the father's impatient tone.
Norpois's deliberate courtesy draws her formally into the conversation as hostess, a quiet mark of inclusion in the valued social exchange.

ambiguities: La grand-mère is mentioned only as the source of secondhand reported speech (via the father) about the narrator's absorption during the play; she is not staged as a direct participant in this scene, so she was left unscored.

The speaker of 'Si elle est très bien, qu'est-ce qu'il te faut de plus ?' is not explicitly tagged; it most plausibly continues the father's impatient interrogation, but if it belongs to someone else the mixed reading of S1 would need adjustment.
